'''''Schoenoplectus triqueter''''', commonly known as the '''triangular [[Schoenoplectus|club-rush]]''', is a species of [[sedge]] which lives in temperate Eurasian wetlands, on muddy shores and river margins. It is found across Eurasia, as well as in South Africa, and has been introduced to North America on the west coast. Because of its tolerance of salty habitats, it is considered a [[halophyte]], but plants which were subjected to a high salinity level (10 parts per thousand) in an experiment were noticeably stunted.

== Description ==
''Schoenoplectus triqueter'' is a medium-sized sedge, growing {{Convert|50–150|cm|ft}} tall, with long, thick (2–10 mm in diameter) rhizomes and thin stems (2–4 mm in diameter).<ref>{{Cite web |title=Schoenoplectus triqueter |url=https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=43578 |access-date=2024-05-23 |website=Jepson eFlora}}</ref> The sedge flowers and fruits in summer; the fruit are small, brown, and bristly.<ref name=":1" /> The flowers are [[Anemophily|wind-pollinated]].<ref name=":4" />

''S. triqueter'' spreads both [[Asexual reproduction|asexually]] through [[rhizome]]s—underground stems which send up new shoots—and [[Sexual reproduction|sexually]] through seeds; it spreads by seed far more in cultivation than in the wild. In fact, no seeds were found during surveys of the wild population around the [[Shannon River Basin|Shannon River]].<ref name=":3" />

=== Effects of salinity ===
A 2005 study looked at the effects of varying levels of [[salinity]] on ''S. triqueter''<nowiki/>'s growth habits. The plants subjected to a salinity level of 10 {{Abbr|ppt|parts per thousand}} had their growth noticeably stunted relative to the [[Scientific control|control sample]]. The plants at 2 ppt, however, were 21% taller with 67%-heavier rhizomes than the control sample.<ref name=":3" /> Another study, in Punjab, found that, in general, the length of the plants' roots consistently increased as the salinity of the soil was raised. Other modifications to the root structure, such as an increase in the area of the [[vascular bundle]]s as the salinity increased. The study concluded that, of the three species it had looked at (''S. triqueter, [[Schoenoplectus juncoides|S. juncoides]],'' and ''[[Schoenoplectus lacustris|S. lacustris]]'') ''S. triqueter'' was the most salt-tolerant, due to its root adapdations. The species is considered a [[halophyte]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Batool |first1=Riffat |last2=Hameed |first2=Mansoor |date=2013 |title=Root structural modifications in three Schoenoplectus (Reichenb.) Palla species for salt tolerance |url=https://academia.edu/download/85496856/17.pdf |journal=Pak. J. Bot. |volume=45 |issue=6}}</ref>

== Distribution and conservation ==
''S. triqueter'' inhabits wetlands, shores, and muddy river banks.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Schoenoplectus triqueter - FNA |url=http://floranorthamerica.org/Schoenoplectus_triqueter |access-date=2024-05-23 |website=floranorthamerica.org}}</ref><ref name="IUCN">{{Cite report |url=http://www.iucnredlist.org/details/164040/0 |title=Schoenoplectus triqueter (Triangular Club-rush) |last=Landsdown |first=R. V. |date=2014 |publisher=International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) |doi=10.2305/iucn.uk.2014-1.rlts.t164040a42376572.en |language=en}}</ref> The species was classified as "[[Least-concern species|Least Concern]]" by the IUCN in 2013. In some regions, it is classified as endangered, and the species has been [[Local extinction|extirpated]] from the Czech Republic.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Schoenoplectus triqueter (L.) Palla {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:1019165-1 |access-date=2024-05-23 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref> ''S. triqueter'' is also known to be in decline in north-central Europe and in the British Isles.<ref name=":3" /> However, it grows prolifically enough in China that it is considered a [[Weed|pest]] in rice paddies.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Deegan |first1=Brian |last2=Harrington |first2=Thomas J. |last3=Dundon |first3=Patrick |date=2005 |title=Effects of salinity and inundation regime on growth and distribution of Schoenoplectus triqueter |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0304377004001858 |journal=Aquatic Botany |language=en |volume=81 |issue=3 |pages=199–211 |doi=10.1016/j.aquabot.2004.11.006|bibcode=2005AqBot..81..199D |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

=== British Isles ===
In the British Isles, although many populations have been lost due to construction projects and [[land reclamation]], populations in Ireland around the [[River Shannon]] persist in some numbers.<ref name=":2" /> The species is classified as critically endangered by the [[Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland]].<ref>{{Citation |title=GB Red List for Vascular Plants |date=2021 |url=https://bsbi.org/download/17380/ |publisher=[[Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland]]}}</ref> It has been suggested that its distribution is restricted due to the plants' low tolerance of [[salinity]].<ref name=":3" /> The main factors driving the species' decline are [[Habitat destruction|habitat loss]], soil [[Soil erosion|erosion]], [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridisation]] with other related species, and the spread of ''[[Phragmites]]'' plants.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rich |first1=T. C. G. |last2=Fitzgerald |first2=R. |date=2002 |title=Life cycle, ecology and distribution of ''Schoenoplectus triqueter'' (L.) Palla (Cyperaceae), Triangular Club-rush, in Britain and Ireland |journal=Watsonia |volume=24 |pages=57–67}}</ref><ref name=":1" /> The last known English population, on the [[River Tamar]], died in 2012, but the species has been successfully re-introduced at ten sites.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=PlantAtlas |url=https://plantatlas2020.org/atlas/2cd4p9h.p5c |access-date=2024-05-24 |website=plantatlas2020.org}}</ref>

=== Mainland Europe ===
In Portugal, the species is classified as vulnerable.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2017-07-11 |title=Schoenoplectus triqueter |url=https://listavermelha-flora.pt/flora-single/ |access-date=2024-05-26 |website=Lista Vermelha da Flora |language=pt}}</ref>

===North America===
In North America, ''S. triqueter'' has been introduced in and around the lower [[Columbia River]] tidal region, where it is known to produce fertile hybrids with ''[[Schoenoplectus tabernaemontani|S. tabernaemontani]]''.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Committee |first=Flora of North America Editorial |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gMtMAgAAQBAJ&dq=%22Schoenoplectus+triqueter%22+%22America%22&pg=PA50 |title=Flora of North America: Volume 23: Magnoliophyta: Commelinidae (in Part): Cyperaceae |date=1993 |publisher=OUP USA |isbn=978-0-19-515207-4 |language=en}}</ref> It is found in southwestern [[Washington (state)|Washington state]] and adjacent parts of [[Oregon]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |title=Schoenoplectus triqueter - Burke Herbarium Image Collection |url=https://burkeherbarium.org/imagecollection/taxon.php?Taxon=Schoenoplectus%20triqueter |access-date=2024-05-30 |website=burkeherbarium.org}}</ref>
